summary:
Subcarpathian Voivodeship stands under the national framework of Poland, where detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals; her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.

The local-authority hostility of the past decade has formally ended. The county of Łańcut in Subcarpathian Voivodeship repealed its anti-LGBT resolution at an extraordinary councillors' session on 27 April 2025, the last such measure in Poland; at the wave's peak about one third of the country's territory was covered by these documents. The voivodeship's own council had already repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution on 20 September 2021, so a visitor arriving now encounters no standing regional declaration of that kind, although the resolutions were political statements rather than entry restrictions.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

The wider legal environment remains in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.
tangentialFactors:
The anti-LGBT resolution wave was a national phenomenon, not a local one. At its peak roughly one third of Poland's territory carried such documents, according to the Atlas of Hate mapping project, and the final repeal came from a county inside Subcarpathian Voivodeship itself, Łańcut, on 27 April 2025.

Podkarpackie Voivodeship's own repeal on 20 September 2021 was part of a coordinated retreat: the councils of Małopolska and Lubelskie repealed comparable resolutions the same day, after the European Commission threatened to withhold regional development funds. Financial leverage, rather than domestic legal change, is what ended the voivodeship-level measures. Podkarpackie replaced its ordinance with a generic anti-discrimination statement.

Human Rights Watch's assessment that reform under the Tusk government has been slow and insufficient through 2024 gives the direction of travel: protections announced at ministerial level have not yet hardened into statute, so a trans visitor should read the current position as an unfinished process rather than a settled one.
localsOnly:
Residents of Subcarpathian Voivodeship live under a regional council decision taken on 20 September 2021 that replaced the 'LGBT-free' resolution with a generic anti-discrimination statement, and under a county-level resolution era that ended when Łańcut repealed its measure on 27 April 2025. No local authority in Poland now holds such a resolution.

Same-sex couples resident in Poland gained a route to the marriage certificates they obtained abroad in June 2024, when Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive of his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition. A framework for registered partnerships remains to be enacted following the European Court of Human Rights ruling of September 2024.

Protection against hate speech on grounds of gender identity and sexual orientation sits in pending legislation: a draft Penal Code amendment raised penalties and cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, a second bill followed in late October 2024, and the Prosecutor General's response team issued new guidelines for law enforcement.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the two hate-speech bills at the time of travel is unresolved in the sources available here; the inventory records the March draft's postponement and the second bill of late October 2024 but no final adoption, so current penalties should be verified rather than assumed.

It is not sourced whether the generic anti-discrimination statement adopted by Podkarpackie Voivodeship in September 2021 names gender identity or trans status, or what practical complaint route it offers.

No trans-specific violence, detention or policing data for Subcarpathian Voivodeship itself appears in the inventory; the documented detention cases are national in scope and are cited here as the pattern a visitor to the voivodeship would stand under.

The sources do not establish whether the Hague route or Polish marriage recognition applies to a trans person's own married status when crossing into the voivodeship, and that question is not resolved here.
